body.p: Applicant amends claim 17 to recite "wherein the probe tip comprises an EEPROM

within the probe tip and wherein a mass of the probe tip is stored on the EEPROM." Basis for the amendment to claim 17 can be found from previously presented claim 20, now cancelled. Applicant respectfully requests entry of the claim amendments.
Upon entry of these amendments, claims 17, 18, and 21-39 are pending with claims 28- 39 being withdrawn.
Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the Office Action mailed August 20, 2024, in view of the foregoing amendments and the remarks provided below.
I. Claim Interpretation - 35 USC §112

Applicant notes that the Examiner has interpreted various features of the claims under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f). Applicant does not concede that 35 U.S.C. §112(f) applies to the features of the claims as filed. Nevertheless, Applicant amends various claims such that 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) does not apply.
II. Claim Rejections - 35 USC §103

Claims 17, 18, and 23-27 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 for being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2009/0171234 to Gurewitsch (hereinafter "Gurewitsch") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2014/0114193 to Anthony (hereinafter "Anthony") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2007/0167819 to Osborn (hereinafter "Osborn) in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,045,517 to Williams (hereinafter "Williams"), in view of US Patent Application Publication No. 2003/0164708 Park (hereinafter "Park"), in view of International Application Publication WO 00/17863 to Beane (hereinafter "Beane"), and in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,258,024 to Van Der Weegan (hereinafter "Van Der Weegan").

Claim 20 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 for being unpatentable over Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Williams, Park, Beane, Van Der Weegan, in view of US Patent Application Publication No. 2012/0187000 Kahn (hereinafter "Kahn"). In the herewith amended claims, the
Page 8of13
language of claim 20 has been included in claim 17 and discussion of the rejections pertaining to claim 20 will be considered in the arguments for claim 17.
Claims 21 and 22 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 for being unpatentable over
Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Williams, Van Der Weegan, in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2013/0217979 to Blackadar (hereinafter "Blackadar").

The pending claims recite an elongate probe that is an electrical impedance spectroscopy probe suitable for investigation the electrical conductivity of cervical tissue. None of the presently cited references, alone or in combination, teach or suggest the combination of elements and the resulting structure of the present claims.

Claim 17, as amended, recites a probe tip with an EEPROM that has the probe tip mass stored thereon. As such, the claimed device does not require calibration to compensate for gravity acting on the probe tip, apart from the calibration of the load cell at device manufacture. With real-time gravity and load cell measurements and known mass of the probe tip, the claimed device can generate fully compensated tip force measurements without further calibration.

The Office Action alleges that "Anthony teaches an apparatus capable of determining a force Ftip applied to a tip of a probe ( 0006 and 0028, determining contact force of a probe). Anthony teaches that the probe comprises a force sensor located in a handle (Fig. 1, force sensor 110 is located in the handle which comprises frame 118 and trunk 140 - see 0008, 0030, and 0033, describing the probe as being handheld))." However, the Applicant disagrees with this interpretation of Anthony, which discloses:

[0033] In one aspect, the frame 118 may be adapted for handheld use, and more particularly adapted for gripping by a technician in the same orientation as a conventional ultrasound probe. Without limitation, this may include a trunk 140 or the like for gripping by a user that extends axially away from the ultrasound transducer 124 and generally normal to the contact surface of the transducer 124.
Stated alternatively, the trunk 140 may extend substantially parallel to the actuation
axis 114 and be shaped and sized for gripping by a human hand.
Figure 1 of Anthony reproduced below for convenience.
Page :10ofl3
The force sensor 110 of Anthony is coupled to the frame 118 (see 0037), which may

include a trunk 140 for gripping (see 0033). A person of ordinary skill in the art would interpret Anthony such that the trunk 140 is analogous to a handle of the device and that the handle (trunk 140) extends axially away from the probe (ultrasound transducer 124). Therefore, a person of ordinary skill in the art would interpret Anthony's handle (trunk 140) to be part of a separate segment of the device from the probe (ultrasound transducer 124). As seen in Figure 1 of Anthony, the force sensor 110 is proximal to the probe 112/transducer 124. Thus, a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand that the force sensor 110 of Anthony is not in the "handle" (trunk 140) of Anthony. The Applicant therefore contends that Anthony does not teach that the probe comprises a force sensor located in a handle, wherein the handle as claimed is attached to the elongate probe.

Further, the Office Action alleges that Anthony teaches "processing means (Fig. 2, [0040], controller 120) for compensating for the mass of the probe tip ( 0059 calibrating the sensors to minimize errors associated with the weight of the probe) using said measured force ... to produce a calibrated measurement of said force Ftip, applied to said probe tip." The applicant respectfully notes that the controller 120 of Anthony ( 0040):

may generally include processing circuitry to control operation of the device 100 as described herein. The controller 120 may receive signals from the sensor 110 indicative of force/torque and from the position sensor 142 of the linear drive system 122 indicative of the position of the probe 112 relative to the travel end points and may generate a control signal to a control input of the linear drive system 122 (or directly to the linear actuator 104) for maintaining a given contact force between the ultrasound probe 112 and the target, as described more fully herein. The controller 120 may include analog or digital circuitry, computer- program code stored in a non-transitory computer-readable storage medium, and the like. Embodiments of the controller 120 may employ pure force control,
impedance control, contact force-determined position control, and the like.
The controller 120 of Anthony does not teach the "a microcontroller for compensating for the mass of the probe tip using said measured force and gravity vector to produce a calibrated

measurement of said force Ftip applied to said probe tip, the microcontroller generating a displayable output for indicating to a user the calibrated measurement of said force Ftip" as claimed. Rather, the controller of Anthony is disclosed as employing "pure force control, impedance control, contact force-determined position control, and the like," which is different than the microcontroller of claim 17 for producing "a calibrated measurement of said force Ftip applied to said probe tip."
The Office Action asserts that "while [Anthony is] not explicit about using an

accelerometer located in the handle in fixed relationship with the probe tip and the load cell for measuring a gravity vector and using the gravity vector in compensating for the mass of the probe," such a teaching could be inferred from 0061 of Anthony. Applicant respectfully disagrees. Anthony discloses at 0044 "Other sensors (indicated generally as a second sensor 138) may be included," and "one or more inertial sensors may be included in the device," which are interpreted to be depicted as second sensors 138. Fig. 1 of Anthony, reproduced above, shows the second sensor near the probe 112 and presumably proximal to the force sensor 110. Because a person of ordinary skill in the art would interpret Anthony's trunk 140 as a handle of the device and the force sensor 110 and the probe 112 are not located in the trunk 140, the second sensor 138 (accelerometer) would also not be located in the handle (trunk 140).

The Office Action fails to show that it would have been prima facie obvious to replace the spring arrangement of Gurewitsch with the force sensor and associated components of Anthony as neither Gurewitsch nor Anthony teaches or discloses a load cell (force sensor) located in the handle nor an accelerometer located in the handle. Further, it would not have been obvious to rely on Anthony to teach an apparatus capable of determining a force Ftip, which the Office conceded Gurewitsch does not explicitly teach.

The Office Action concedes that Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Park, and Beane do not appear to explicitly teach that the probe tip is an interchangeable probe tip removably attached to said handle. The Office Action relies on Van Der Weegen to teach a removable probe engaged with a re-usable hand piece comprising a handle. However, a device based on the teachings of Gurewitsch and Anthony would need to be adapted to use an interchangeable probe tip because, as demonstrated above, neither Gurewitsch nor Anthony teaches or discloses a load cell (force sensor) located in the handle nor an accelerometer located in the handle. Rather, the teachings of

Anthony lead to a device with a force sensor and accelerometer located proximal to the probe. Therefore, applying an interchangeable probe tip, as Van Der Weegen allegedly teaches, to the device of Gurewitsch and Anthony would not lead to an apparatus recited in claim 17 comprising a handle; an elongate probe comprising said probe tip attached to said handle; a load cell located in said handle (Anthony teaches a force sensor proximate to the probe, not in the handle); an accelerometer located in the handle (Anthony teaches a force sensor proximate to the probe, not in the handle); wherein said probe tip is an interchangeable probe tip removably attached to said handle.

The Office Action alleges that Kahn teaches an EEPROM to store probe calibration parameters (Fig. 3, 0251 and 0407). Kahn ( 0407) discloses that "the sensor or holder can have on-board electronic memory, such as [EEPROM]." Kahn does not teach or suggest using an EEPROM within any particular segment of the device, let alone the probe tip, wherein a mass of the probe tip is stored on the EEPROM and wherein the probe tip is interchangeable. In the claimed device, the EEPROM within the probe tip and storing the mass provides a technical benefit of being able to access the mass of the probe tip for compensating the mass of the probe tip using said measured force and gravity vector, such that each probe tip may have slight variations of mass, which if approximated, would decrease the accuracy and precision of the device that is intended to detect small changes in electrical impedance.

For the reasons provided above, Applicant submits that claim 17 is not rendered obvious by the teachings of Kahn in combination with Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Park, Beane, and Van Der Weegen and respectfully request the rejection be withdrawn.
In view of the above, Applicant submits that claims 17, 18 and 21-27 are allowable over the cited references.
III. Double Patenting

The claims have been provisionally rejected on the grounds of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claims 1-9 of U.S. Patent No. 11,660,046 Anumba (hereinafter "Anumba") in view of Gurewitsch, Anthony, Osborn, Williams, Van Der Weegan, Park, Kahn, Blackadar as outlined previously. The applicant respectfully requests the grounds of rejection be deferred until all other matters of substance have been resolved.

Applicant respectfully submits that the claims are allowable for the reasons provided herein. If the Examiner wishes to discuss the application or the remarks provided herein, the Examiner is urged to contact the undersigned at the direct number below.

No fees are believed to be due; however, the Commissioner is hereby authorized to charge any additional fees that may be required by this paper, or credit any overpayment, to Deposit Account No. 50-5226.
